newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Quiet Buddhist farewell for mercy death Australian.
newsitem.headline: Quiet Buddhist farewell for mercy death Australian.

text.p: Friends and family of the first man to die under Australia's unique voluntary euthanasia law packed a tin-shed Buddhist temple on Friday to bid farewell to a man described as brave and devoted to helping others.
About 200 people, all barefoot, knelt or sat cross-legged while monks chanted prayers and friends praised 66-year-old carpenter and one-time Christian missionary Bob Dent.
They included Philip Nitschke, the local doctor who helped Dent die under the Northern Territory's assisted-suicide law.

Dent, terminally-ill with prostate cancer, died on Sunday from a computer-delivered lethal injection, becoming the first person to use the law since it came into effect in this outback region in July.
His death has renewed debate in Australia and beyond on the issue of "mercy killings".

The architect of the law, former Northern Territory government chief Marshall Perron, urged Australians on Friday to lobby their national parliamentarians to reject calls to overturn the territory legislation.
A conservative backbencher, backed by Prime Minister John Howard, has launched a private bid in the federal parliament to have Canberra use its constitutional powers to quash the law.
The law faces a separate threat in the High Court, Australia's highest court, where a coalition of doctors, church and Aboriginal leaders is seeking to have it declared unconstitutional.
Media were barred from Dent's 30-minute funeral service and reporters, photographers and television crews looked on through a wire-mesh fence topped by barbed wire.
Dent turned to Buddhism after he was diagnosed with prostate cancer five years ago. He went on to become a leading figure in the local Buddhist community.
"Today, we farewell a gentleman, a craftsman and a very generous individual," said an unidentified man heard by reporters over a loudspeaker system from the temple.
"This gentleman devoted most of his time to helping other people. His acceptance and lack of fear of the inevitable should be a good example and inspiration to us all."
Another mourner told the crowd: "By such acts we perform today, we all wish him happiness and peace."
After the service, Dent's coffin was placed before a seven metre-high gold Buddhist spire he had built while dying, as the crowd stood for three minutes' silence in sweltering heat.
Nitschke walked in front of the coffin carrying a photo of Dent in the procession from the temple to the spire, or stupa.
Dent's coffin was taken to a nearby crematorium, where more Buddhist blessings followed. However, family, friends and crematorium officials refused to say whether Dent had been cremated.

Local government sources said earlier that a legal glitch might delay his cremation. Under local law, people can only be cremated if they have died of natural causes, unless a coroner gives a special authorisation.
